11881-the-shadow-of-the-north-a-story-of:
Joseph A. Altsheler's 1917 novel belongs to his French and Indian War series, following Robert Lennox, a lad of unknown origin, Tayoga, a young Onondaga warrior, and the hunter David Willet. A long cast list sets them among French officers, British generals, and Mohawk leaders such as Joseph Brant.

The story moves between old New York and wilderness campaigns, with blockhouses, pack horses, and rifle work in the forest. Altsheler treats the lost campaign of the title as a test of loyalty and endurance, where young soldiers learn war not from parade grounds but from cold, distance, and sudden attack.
1217-penelope-s-experiences-in-scotland-:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sends Penelope, her American traveler, to Scotland, where she tours castles, lochs, and villages and writes home in letters full of humor and affection. The tale follows Penelope and her friends through Edinburgh, the Highlands, and country inns, meeting lairds, guides, and ghosts.

Wiggin writes Scotland with a tourist's delight and a novelist's eye for character. The book is light, sunny, and full of local color. It suits readers who like gentle travel tales and the Scotland of storybooks. Wiggin's Scotland letters still charm travelers and armchair tourists alike.
12518-the-adventures-of-a-forty-niner-an:
Daniel Knower's 1894 account describes California and San Francisco in the gold-rush years, through events and ideas of those early days. Knower dedicates the book to Stevenson, Frémont and Sutter, three pre-eminent pioneers of California, and recalls a society formed to preserve the memory of that time.

Membership in that society required arrival in California before 1 January 1850, a rule that marks the forty-niner generation. Knower writes of camps, streets, people and customs, mixing personal memory with history. The book serves as a vivid, partisan record of a city built in haste, told by a man who was there.
131-the-pilgrim-s-progress-from-this-wor:
Christian flees the City of Destruction with a burden on his back and a book in his hand. John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, told as a dream, follows him toward the Celestial City. The Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, and the Giant Despair block his road.

Faithful, Hopeful, and Evangelist help or warn him, while flatterers and tyrants mislead him. Bunyan's allegory turns doctrine into inns, hills, and battles a reader can picture. Part One stands complete on its own. The book became, after the Bible, the most read work in English.
1358-enoch-arden-c:
Alfred Tennyson's poem tells of Enoch Arden, a fisherman who sails and is wrecked, spending years marooned on a desert island while his wife Annie, believing him dead, marries his friend Philip. Enoch returns at last, sees his wife happy, and chooses silence over ruin.

Tennyson writes the tale in blank verse of grave beauty, and Enoch's self-denial gives it its pathos. The poem was a bestseller in its day and inspired plays and films. It remains a moving study of love, loss, and noble restraint. Tennyson's verse gives Enoch's self-denial its full pathos.
13589-the-theory-of-the-theatre-and-othe:
Clayton Hamilton's Theory of the Theatre and Other Principles of Dramatic Criticism, uniform with his Studies in Stagecraft, examines how plays work on stage. The companion volume covers the new art of making plays, the pictorial stage, the decorative drama, and the drama of illusion. It also covers stage direction and a plea for a new type of play.

Hamilton describes an Elizabethan stage with an arras drawn aside to reveal a bed or banqueting board. An upper room serves for Juliet's balcony or a commandant on city walls, and properties move on and off like the trellised arbor in The Spanish Tragedy. A dramatist, he warns, is at actors' mercy: a delicate love scene can be spoiled by an actor without feeling, or a cruel character softened by too charming a player.
17374-bank-of-the-manhattan-company-char:
The Bank of the Manhattan Company, of 40 Wall Street, New York, issued this account of its origin, history, and progress, as a progressive commercial bank chartered in 1799. The story opens on May 8, 1799, when the committee on by-laws reported a common seal for the corporation, showing Oceanus, a god of the sea, seated in state. That old seal marks a bank born with the young republic.

Readers follow the bank from its charter through growth into a major New York institution, with attention to its business and its place in the city. The volume serves local historians, banking historians, and anyone curious about how an early American bank presented its own past. Its tone is proud, as befits a corporate history.
17546-the-lion-of-saint-mark-a-story-of-:
G. A. Henty set this adventure story in Venice in the fourteenth century, under the sign of the Lion of Saint Mark. Chapters open with Venice itself and a conspiracy, then move to the Grand Canal, a carrying off, a clue, and a hut on San Nicolo. A trader's ship, an attack by pirates, the capture of the Lido, and a recapture follow, with battles at Antium and Pola ahead.

Young readers follow a hero through Venetian politics, sea fights, and escapes, in Henty's brisk, instructive style. The book mixes history with adventure, teaching something of Venice's power while keeping the pace quick. It remains a sturdy example of Henty's historical tales for boys.
17973-the-world-of-romance-being-contrib:
William Morris wrote The World of Romance, gathering his tales from the Oxford and Cambridge Magazine of 1856, printed in London in 1906 by J. Thomson. Morris, still a student, had paid for the magazine himself, with Rossetti among its writers, and it ran just twelve issues.

The tales live in pure romance: medieval customs, buildings, faith, and the social frame of the 1200s and 1300s, set in no known age or land. The Story of the Unknown Church opens the set, told by a mason whose church vanished two centuries past. Morris later called these tales crude and young, yet they glow with his early fire.
18696-the-olden-time-series-vol-6-litera:
Henry M. Brooks compiled this sixth volume of Ye Olden Time Series at Boston in 1886 with Ticknor and Company. The series gleans items from old newspapers, chiefly of Boston and Salem, with brief comments by Brooks. Earlier volumes covered lotteries, spinning wheels, Sundays, advertisements, and punishments; this one turns to literary curiosities.

An index of names runs from John Adams and Anne Bradstreet to Benedict Arnold and Major Andre, showing the range of scraps within. Brooks offers amusement for young and old plus raw stuff for students of New England history. The book is a charming dip into old print culture.
19422-the-organization-of-the-congregati:
Beale M. Schmucker wrote this study of how early Lutheran congregations in America formed and governed themselves, first printed in a church review in the late eighteen hundreds. Free from state control for the first time, these groups had to settle their own rules for pastors, members, and church order.

The study draws on early constitutions, including that of Augustus Church, and on the work of Henry Muhlenberg in shaping common practice. It shows how a shared confession, above all the Augsburg Confession, gave scattered immigrant churches a common frame without a state church to hold them.
19765-vikings-of-the-pacific-the-adventu:
A. C. Laut's Vikings of the Pacific, from 1905, tells of explorers who came to America's West Coast. Laut opens with a credo: man can become master of his destiny. We forget, she writes, that people can fight and remake their own surroundings. Her explorers are exhibits for that claim. They are the sea rovers and fur traders of the North Pacific.

Laut wrote popular history with a novelist's pace. Russian, Spanish, British, and American adventurers crowd these coasts. Their story runs from Bering's voyages toward settled trade. She treats them as Vikings for their daring, not their blood. The book is romantic history, proud and brisk. It preserves an early Canadian voice on the Pacific past.
19768-professor-royce-s-libel-a-public-a:
Professor Royce's Libel is a public appeal for redress addressed to Harvard University. Its author felt attacked in print and little defended. He writes that speaking out would seem needless if Harvard itself were not involved. An attack otherwise unworthy of notice drew his answer for that reason. The pamphlet is self-defense conducted before the public. Academic honor in that era was fought in pamphlets.

Such appeals were the op-eds of the nineteenth century. A scholar's name was his capital, and libel threatened it directly. The author asks the university community to judge his case. Readers meet the raw etiquette of old academic feuds. The heat is real, even when the cause is forgotten.
20136-the-seventeenth-highland-light-inf:
The Seventeenth Highland Light Infantry, Glasgow Chamber of Commerce Battalion, kept a war history. Its field narrative stays close to the battalion's own share of the campaign. The history committee barred any wide view of the whole war. Other units and grand strategy sit outside its chosen scope.

Glasgow raised this battalion from its chamber of commerce circles. Clerks and business men served in its ranks on the western front. Unit histories like this one list actions, losses, and names with care. They let families trace where their men fought, fell, and endured.
20322-notes-and-queries-number-188-june-:
Notes and Queries, number 188, for June 4, 1853, is a journal of shared learning. Its subtitle calls it a medium of inter-communication for literary men. Readers wrote in with questions, answers, and small finds on books and history. One note quotes a writer who vows to fix two faulted lines.

He will let his enemy do him a kindness where harm was meant. Such exchanges built a vast store of notes on words, graves, and customs. Scholars and keen amateurs still mine old Notes and Queries volumes. This number gives a neat taste of Victorian learning by post.
20361-the-voice-of-the-machines-an-intro:
The Voice of the Machines introduces the twentieth century through its machines. The machine, it argues, is a wholly new fact in human life. In importance and in shaping daily life, it has no precedent. The machine has no traditions of its own to draw on.

To take a traditional stand on life, one must leave the machine out. It has always been left out, the writer notes with irony. Yet leaving it out now changes little, as machines rule more. Readers get an early, sharp essay on technology's rise and its cost.
20408-notes-and-queries-number-185-may-1:
Dated May 14, 1853, number 185 of Notes and Queries carries the usual mix of queries, replies, and short learned notes. Its readers chased exact facts about books, authors, inscriptions, and customs. No topic was too small if it could be settled by proof.

One note marvels at the fate of the Emblems of Alciatus. The book passed through countless editions and was translated into most languages of the continent. Yet no version was ever printed in England, though English readers knew the work. The item shows the journal at work on the odd gaps in book history.
20409-notes-and-queries-number-186-may-2:
Number 186 of Notes and Queries came out on May 21, 1853. Like every issue, it prints brief notes and answers sent in by readers. Church history, old authors, and points of language all find a place in its columns.

One note corrects every edition of a work that prints the name Osorius. The name, the writer argues, must be a mere misprint. The man was no Portuguese bishop but a Spaniard, born at Tarragona. Other notes follow Saint Augustine on a mission to Jerusalem. The issue shows Victorian scholars mending small errors with great care.
20410-notes-and-queries-number-187-may-2:
Number 187 of Notes and Queries is dated May 28, 1853. The journal served as a shared notebook for readers who studied old books and records. Its pages carry queries, replies, and corrections from across the country.

One note takes up the memoir printed with the 1845 Aldine edition of Chaucer's poems. There Sir Harris Nicolas argues that Chaucer did not know the Italian language. If true, the poet could not have drawn directly on Italian books. The note shows how the journal's readers tested big claims about famous authors against hard evidence. Small facts, firmly settled, were the journal's pride.
21894-the-rover-boys-at-colby-hall-or-th:
A second generation of Rovers goes to school in The Rover Boys at Colby Hall, by Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer. Tom Rover's twins are chips of the old block, Sam Rover says, with a capital I. The frontispiece shows Jack Rover starting down the football field with the ball. Colby Hall is a military school, and its young cadets struggle through studies, sports, and scrapes.

Stratemeyer built the Rover Boys into one of the best-loved boys' series in America. This volume opens the second series, handing the flag to the sons of the first heroes. The formula is intact: clean fun, loyal friends, and bullies beaten fairly. Generations of boys learned series reading on books like this one.
22117-across-coveted-lands-or-a-journey-:
A. Henry Savage Landor crossed Asia in the journey told in Across Coveted Lands. His route ran overland from Flushing in Holland all the way to Calcutta. He left his baggage registered for Warsaw, crossed by night boat, and sped by express through Berlin. Ahead lay Russia, Persia, and Baluchistan, lands coveted by rival empires.

Landor describes courts, deserts, caravans, and the politics of the Great Game. Britain and Russia watched every road he travelled. His drawings and photographs filled the published volumes. Landor was a showman as well as a traveller, and his books sold adventure with real geography. This one covers the classic overland route to India.
22126-notes-and-queries-number-35-june-2:
Notes and Queries was a weekly paper where scholars answered each other's questions by post. Number 35, dated June 29, 1850, shows the young journal at work. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, is "When found, make a note of." Antiquaries, genealogists, and literary men crowd its columns.

One note untangles two Gorings, father and son, both Earls of Norwich in the Civil War years. Careless compilers had merged the men; a careful reader separates them. Around such notes sit queries on proverbs, books, inscriptions, and family arms. The journal trained Victorian scholarship to work in public. Single issues like this one are bricks in that great shared notebook.
22127-notes-and-queries-number-34-june-2:
Number 34 of Notes and Queries appeared on June 22, 1850, in the journal's first year. The weekly paper linked literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists across Britain. Readers sent questions; other readers answered them in print. Its notes open with Henry Nicholas, founder of the Family of Love.

Nicholas, a Westphalian who lived at Amsterdam and Emden, styled himself a deified man. The note traces his sect's strange career from about 1540. Other columns handle ballads, epitaphs, and points of local history. Reading one issue shows the machine working: small facts, carefully checked, passed hand to hand. Notes and Queries ran for more than a century on that simple plan.
22793-the-standard-oratorios-their-stori:
George P. Upton wrote The Standard Oratorios: Their Stories, Their Music, and Their Composers, a handbook for concert-goers in the great age of choral societies. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. When every city had its Handel festival, listeners needed a guide to the works, their plots, and their makers.

The preface promises that each oratorio is described as fully as its brief allotment of space allows. The author says the utmost pains went into historical and chronological accuracy. Such details, he notes, are nearly always matters of controversy. Handel, Haydn, and Mendelssohn anchor the canon the book surveys. Upton wrote a shelf of such standard guides, and this one taught Victorian and American audiences how to hear their favorite sacred dramas.
23204-notes-and-queries-number-70-march-:
Number 70 of Notes and Queries, dated March 1, 1851, is one issue of a weekly journal where readers traded notes, questions, and answers on books, history, and old customs. One item in this issue makes a grand appeal. Its writer calls on the literary men of England, the government, and the public to back a glorious expedition.

He urges them to keep in mind words set at the head of his article, drawn from a much-loved author. The mix is typical of the journal: bold public proposals sit beside small points of learning. Readers get a lively record of Victorian curiosity at work.
23205-notes-and-queries-number-71-march-:
Number 71 of Notes and Queries, dated March 8, 1851, continues the weekly exchange of literary notes and questions. One note turns to Shakespeare. Its writer picks out a few passages in All's Well That Ends Well that, he says, have had little light thrown on them despite all that has been written.

The passage in question shows Bertram pressing Diana to give in to his wishes. Notes like this were the journal's trade: a reader flags a hard line, and other readers answer in later issues. The result is a slow, public seminar on classic texts, run in print.
23402-notes-and-queries-number-75-april-:
Notes and Queries, a weekly medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, filled this number of early April, eighteen fifty one, with notes, queries, and replies. Its motto bids the reader, when found, make a note of it, and the pages live up to that call.

Inside, Edward Foss writes on two chancellors, Bolton Corney on a Carolina lament, and folk lore notes cover cures for whooping cough, Devon charms, and Lent lilies. Queries chase poems of John Seguard of Norwich, an epitaph for the Countess of Pembroke, the sense of a word, and the arms of Robert Nelson. For lovers of old books and odd facts, the issue is a lively window onto Victorian learned talk.
23956-anti-slavery-opinions-before-the-y:
William Frederick Poole, librarian of the Public Library of Cincinnati, read Anti-Slavery Opinions Before the Year 1800 before the Cincinnati Literary Club on November 16, 1872. Robert Clarke and Company published it in 1873, with a facsimile reprint of an even rarer document appended.

Poole examines anti-slavery opinion in America just before 1800, using a rare pamphlet from George Washington's library, then kept at the Boston Athenaeum, which had bought the collection in 1849. The appendix reprints Dr. George Buchanan's oration on the moral and political evil of slavery, delivered at Baltimore on July 4, 1791, before the Maryland Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery.
25683-the-escape-of-a-princess-pat-being:
George Pearson tells the escape of a Princess Pat soldier in this full account. Corporal Edwards served in Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. He was captured and held fifteen months. He then escaped from Germany into Holland. Corporal, now Sergeant, Edward Edwards fronts the book in a portrait.

Chapters open at Polygon Wood, Ypres, and Hill 60, preparing for gas, then the fourth of May and an unofficial armistice. Corporal Edwards takes up the tale among the wounded, and Major Gault comes back with news of a king dead and a king living. Capture, prison, and a final dash to Holland close a First World War memoir.
25894-the-spirit-proper-to-the-times-a-s:
James Walker preached this sermon at King's Chapel, Boston, on Sunday, May 12, 1861, at the start of the Civil War. Taking for his text the verse that God is well pleased with such sacrifices, Walker speaks of public spirit as a willingness to give up goods for the public good. Since no one can have everything, he says, we must yield some things to gain or secure others.

Walker notes that wicked men and worldly men both live by sacrifice, the one giving health and name to vice, the miser giving all that makes life worth having to his hoard. The country at war asks sacrifices of property, labor, and life, and Walker finds men ready to give, not grudgingly or of necessity. Printed at the wardens' request, the sermon calls a prosperous nation to bear war's cost with open hands.
27538-notes-and-queries-no-209-october-2:
Notes and Queries, a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, published this number, 209, on Saturday, 29 October 1853, at fourpence. Its motto comes from Captain Cuttle: when found, make a note of.

Notes in this number treat the Scottish national records, Patrick Carey, an inedited lyric by Felicia Hemans, and Shakespeare correspondence. Minor notes cover monumental inscriptions, Marlborough at Blenheim, and the etymology of till and until. Queries ask about polarised light and dramatic representations. The issue shows Victorian scholarship in weekly conversation with itself. Green Eyes, by Harry Leroy Temple, gets a note too.
27583-the-importance-of-the-proof-reader:
John Wilson, formerly proprietor of the University Press, read this paper on the importance of the proof-reader before the Club of Odd Volumes in Boston. The University Press published it in Cambridge in 1901, and reprinted it in 1922 after Wilson's death in 1903.

Wilson names author, compositor, and proof-reader as the three makers of a book in press. The true proof-reader, he argues, should be a practical printer and also a lover of literature, at home in the classics of every tongue and in science's results. His paper draws on fifty years in the printing trade, and defends a craft readers seldom notice.
27629-captain-desmond-v-c:
Maud Diver, author of The Great Amulet and Candles in the Wind, published this revised edition of Captain Desmond, V.C., in large part rewritten, with William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London in 1917. She dedicates it to her son Cyril and to Mrs. Alan Batten, for generous help and interest.

Diver's epigraph, from Robert Browning, praises a man who never retreats, but marches breast forward, and never doubts the clouds will break. In revising, she brought the aftermath nearer her original conception, replacing one final scene with three short chapters. She had suppressed them at first for fear of making the book too long, and risked upsetting the balance of sympathy.
27679-uncle-sam-s-boys-as-sergeants-or-h:
H. Irving Hancock, author of Uncle Sam's Boys in the Ranks and Uncle Sam's Boys in the Philippines, published this boys' army story with Henry Altemus of Philadelphia in 1911, illustrated. Its heroes handle their first real commands as sergeants.

Chapters open with a tip-off by wig-wag, Lieutenant Algy joining the army, and the first breath against a soldier's honor. Corporal Hal's admission, the squad room turning cold, and the racking of the new sergeant follow. Sergeant Overton and discipline, Hal riding into treachery, and chasing a speeding deserter come later. A frontispiece shows Private Hinkey howling: Hey, you idiot.
28474-notes-and-queries-number-192-july-:
Saturday, July 2, 1853, brought number 192 of Notes and Queries, a weekly medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at fourpence. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, reads: When found, make a note of it.

Notes in this number include the oblation of a white bull, Newstead Abbey, and celebrated passages in Romeo and Juliet and King Lear. Queries ask whether Captain Cook first discovered the Sandwich Islands and about superstitions of Cornish miners. Replies, photographic correspondence, and notices to correspondents fill out a lively record of Victorian scholarly curiosity in miniature.
28475-notes-and-queries-number-193-july-:
July 9, 1853, saw number 193 of Notes and Queries, the weekly journal for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at fourpence. Its notes open with the eye and its primary idea, followed by gossiping history, De Quincey's account of Hatfield, and the names of early inhabitants of Hellas.

Shakespeare Readings number nine and Goethe's author-remuneration follow, with minor notes on parallel passages, unpublished epitaphs, and Napoleon's bees. The main query asks whether Thomas Lord Lyttelton wrote Junius's letters. Replies on wild plants, heraldry, and serpents, with photographic correspondence on the camera obscura, complete the number.
29412-the-phantom-world-or-the-philosoph:
Augustine Calmet's Phantom World, translated from the French with a preface and notes by the Rev. Henry Christmas, surveys the history and philosophy of spirits and apparitions. The Philadelphia edition of 1850, two volumes in one, opens with good angels proved from the Old and New Testaments, then moves through apparitions, hauntings, and the claims of the unseen. Christmas, librarian of Sion College, frames Calmet's learning with English notes.

Calmet argues with care: many tales of spirits rest on error, yet behind most human errors lies some grain of truth. The book weighs scripture, history, and reason side by side. Students of folklore, demonology, and the history of belief will find a learned, sober classic on why ghosts have haunted human thought for so long.
30914-the-corner-house-girls-growing-up-:
Grace Brooks Hill wrote this 1918 book in the Corner House Girls series, published by Barse and Hopkins in Newark and New York, with pictures by R. Emmett Owen. Earlier books in the series include The Corner House Girls, The Corner House Girls at School, Under Canvas, In a Play, Odd Find, and On a Tour. The frontispiece shows Ruth springing forward and seizing an old gentleman's coat.

Chapters run from All Up in the Air and The Old Gentleman with the Green Umbrella. They pass through The Aerial Tramway, School in the Offing, The Shepards, Naming the New Baby, and A Feline Furor. They continue with Neighbor, Everything at Sixes and at Sevens, Aboard the Nancy Hanks, and Afloat on the Canal. They end with Missing and The Hue and Cry. It is a sequel in a long-running girls' series, following the Corner House girls as they grow up.
31378-notes-and-queries-number-237-may-1:
Dated Saturday, May 13, 1854, issue number 237 of Notes and Queries presents itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, credited to Captain Cuttle, runs "When found, make a note of." Contents include a note on Shakespeare's rime made at the Mytre by Dr. E. F. Rimbault, a piece on Rous, the Scottish psalmist and provost of Eton, and original English royal letters to the grand masters of Malta by William Winthrop.

Notes, minor queries, and replies fill the rest of the issue, with readers asking and answering questions on history, language, and antiquities. The weekly format made it a clearinghouse for small facts that larger books overlooked. For modern researchers, the issue is a compact record of what Victorian antiquaries were curious about, week by week.
31398-notes-and-queries-number-238-may-2:
Dated Saturday, May 20, 1854, issue number 238 of Notes and Queries presents itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, credited to Captain Cuttle, runs "When found, make a note of." Short notes, minor queries, and replies fill its pages. The contents list ranges from a foreign newspaper leader on the new Russian manifesto to the launch of the Prince Royal in 1610.

Readers also find notes on the Ormulum, the legend of the Seven Sisters, and replies on subjects as varied as Welsh consonants, the screw propeller, and Shelley's Prometheus Unbound. The mix shows how Victorian readers traded facts, asked for help, and corrected one another in print. For anyone tracing a word, a family, or an old custom, the issue is a window onto mid-nineteenth-century antiquarian conversation.
31690-notes-and-queries-number-239-may-2:
Notes and Queries, number 239, for Saturday, May 27, 1854, presents itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, credited to Captain Cuttle, bids the reader to make a note when a thing is found. The number sold for fourpence, fivepence for the stamped edition.

Its notes include reprints of early Bibles by the Reverend R. Hooper, the marriage licence of John Gower the poet, a note on Aska or Asca, legends of the county Clare, and archaic words. Minor notes take up inscriptions on buildings, epitaphs, and numbers. The issue shows the journal's work of query, answer, and shared note-taking.
31885-bible-myths-and-their-parallels-in:
T. W. Doane's Bible Myths and Their Parallels in Other Religions, in its seventh edition with numerous illustrations, compares myths and miracles of the Old and New Testaments with those of ancient heathen nations. It also considers their origin and meaning. Its epigraph, from Professor Max Müller, holds that he who knows only one religion knows none.

Doane says the material was first accumulated for his private use. Most of what it holds can be found spread across hundreds of old and new volumes, yet no earlier work had followed these myths alone as its own book. Readers get a pioneering comparative work, arguing that Bible stories parallel older myths, written for readers willing to follow evidence across cultures.
32423-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with Coucy-le-Château, a northern French village, and runs through entries in the C range. Its index pages list subjects as varied as Cranbrook, Crane, Croatia-Slavonia, Crocodile, and Crockett, alongside legal and historical entries such as Council, Count, and Covenant. Each article gives the concise, sourced treatment that made the eleventh edition a standard reference.

Readers will find biography, geography, science, and history side by side, from artists and soldiers to animals, places, and institutions. The text preserves the edition's spelling, cross-references, and scholarly tone, with transcribers' notes on symbols and corrections. It works as a browsable reference volume and as a record of knowledge as it stood in the early twentieth century.
32807-freehold-land-societies-their-hist:
J. Ewing Ritchie explains the Freehold Land Movement in this pamphlet, published by William Tweedie in 1853 at twopence. The pages were reprinted from the Weekly News and Chronicle, the paper that called itself the organ of the movement.

Ritchie tells what the societies are, what they have done, and what they seek to do. Born of a working man, the movement offers working men independence, wealth, and political power. Members save together to buy land, and a forty-shilling freehold entitles a man to vote for the county. Ritchie weighs the scheme as an investment, a moral school, and a political force.
33631-the-story-of-a-strange-career-bein:
Edited by Stanley Waterloo, this 1902 volume presents itself as the authentic autobiography of a convict, and its career is indeed strange. The narrator, of an old New York family on his mother's side and a Dublin-born father, goes to sea young. He whales in the South Pacific, serves in Her Majesty's service, endures the cat-o'-nine-tails, and escapes. He survives as the sport of the waves.

Later chapters carry him through the New York draft riots, service as an acting ensign in the United States Navy, blockade running, prisoner-of-war life in Libby Prison, Fort Fisher, and Haiti. Later chapters also carry finally westward after leaving the sea. The narrative mixes adventure with prison experience, offering a picaresque life told in the first person. Readers should take its claim of authenticity as the book's own framing, not as settled fact.
34175-domestic-animals-history-and-descr:
R. L. Allen wrote this history and description of domestic animals, published in New York in 1865 by Orange Judd, entered under copyright in 1847. Allen, author of a Compend of American Agriculture, treats the horse, mule, cattle, sheep, swine, poultry, and farm dogs. He gives directions for management, breeding, crossing, rearing, feeding, and preparation for a profitable market. Farmers learn to keep stock healthy, raise young well, and sell at a gain.

Diseases and remedies follow, with full directions for managing the dairy. Allen writes for farmers who want sound, practical knowledge. The book remains a useful record of nineteenth-century American farming practice.
35646-hand-book-of-practical-cookery-for:
A cookery manual by Pierre Blot, founder of the New York Cooking Academy. D Appleton and Company issued the New York edition in 1884. The first copyright dates to 1867. The subtitle promises the whole science and art of preparing human food. Blot addresses ladies and professional cooks alike.

His preface treats food as the first of human wants. A cookbook, he says, resembles a chemistry text. Theory must blend with practice to be useful. It must also fit the products and climate of its country. Blot scorns mere compilers and their repeated receipts. His own are complete, practical, and simple. Any housekeeper, however new, should manage them.
35752-blacker-s-art-of-fly-making-c:
Blacker's Art of Fly Making is an angling manual by Blacker, fishing tackle maker of 54 Dean Street, Soho, London, rewritten and revised by the author in 1855. It was patronised by Prince Albert. The book comprises angling and the dyeing of colours, with engravings of salmon and trout flies. The plates show the process of the gentle craft as taught in the pages.

The contents give an easy method to make the trout fly and a plain salmon fly. The palmer, or double-hackle fly, and the gaudy salmon fly follow. A catechism of fly-making tests the learner. Trout flies for the season are listed month by month, from March onward. Fishing rods and fly fishing for salmon, an account of the salmon and its varieties, and the salmon fry come next.
36415-great-lent-a-school-of-repentance-:
Great Lent, a School of Repentance, by Bishop Alexander Schmemann, was put out in New York in 1970 by the Orthodox Church in America, with a second printing in 1977. Schmemann writes on what Great Lent means for Orthodox Christians. The book is short and clear.

Parts treat the Sundays of preparation, Lenten worship, and how to keep Great Lent. He opens with a hymn for the first week, on fasting in body and in spirit. Lent, he says, is the time of turning back to God, and turning back is the start of true Christian life. Christ first word of preaching was repent. Schmemann calls Lent a school that each Christian must enter each year. Church readers get plain, deep help for the fast.
36555-guide-to-the-kindergarten-and-inte:
Guide to the Kindergarten and Intermediate Class is a teaching manual by Elizabeth Peabody. Mary Mann's Moral Culture of Infancy is bound with it. Steiger published this revised edition in New York in 1877. The book had been in the market since 1860 under its earlier title. A preface dated 1869 opens Peabody's guide. She meant it for those who undertake kindergarten culture. She had been in Europe since the first edition, she writes. There she studied the kindergarten in its homeland.

Peabody was America's leading advocate of Froebel's kindergarten. Mann writes on the moral culture of infancy beside her. The joint volume joins method to moral purpose in teaching. Songs, gifts, and occupations of the kindergarten fill the guide. The revised edition kept the work current for American teachers.
36572-what-and-where-is-god-a-human-answ:
Richard Larue Swain wrote What and Where Is God, published at New York in October nineteen twenty. The subtitle calls it a human answer to the deep religious cry of the modern soul. Swain gave the book to his father's family and his own.

Chapter one studies an honest atheist who lost God through false views of faith. Chapter two asks what, who, and where God is, and what God does. It asks if modern folk are simply making their God, as the ancients made theirs. Later chapters treat the soul, man's place in the universe, and whether God could become a man. The Trinity and the standing of Jesus get close study.
37403-notes-and-queries-number-85-june-1:
Notes and Queries, number 85, came out on Saturday, June 14, 1851, as part of volume three. The weekly paper called itself a means of talk among literary men, artists, antiquaries, and family historians, and it cost threepence. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, was simple: when found, make a note of it.

The number opens with notes on Chaucer and on folk words, and a note on an old man whose father lived in the time of Oliver Cromwell. Queries ask about the Princesses of Wales, old arms, well chapels, and the Devil's Bit. Minor notes touch Sedley, Romeo and Juliet, and a tablet in Limerick Cathedral. Each short item invites a reply from some reader who knows more.
38090-nurses-papers-on-tuberculosis-read:
Nurses' Papers on Tuberculosis gathers talks read before a nurses' study circle in Chicago. The City of Chicago Municipal Tuberculosis Sanitarium issued the set in September 1914. It is the first bulletin of the Dispensary Department, and a long staff list opens the book.

Rosalind Mackay heads the nurses as superintendent, and some fifty dispensary nurses are named under her. The board lists Theodore Sachs as president and Frank Wing as executive officer, with offices on West Monroe Street. The papers came from a study circle formed so that nurses could present work on set phases of the disease. Each nurse took a topic and read her findings to the group. The set shows how a big city fought consumption house by house.
38106-ingersollia-gems-of-thought-from-t:
Gems of thought from the lectures, speeches, and conversations of Robert Ingersoll were gathered in 1882 under the title Ingersollia, as a record of his opinions and beliefs. An editor signing himself Elmo made the choice. The first section is called the romance of farm life, and opens on Ingersoll as a farmer.

He recalls hauling wheat two hundred miles in wagons to sell at thirty-five cents a bushel. The money came home as lumber, shingles, a barrel of salt, and a cook-stove that never would draw and never did bake. Corn and bacon were the fare, and cooking an unknown art. Against that hardness he sets the quiet of the farm and its hope of a serene old age.
38273-is-the-bible-indictable-being-an-e:
Annie Besant's pamphlet asks whether the Bible itself could be indicted as obscene literature. The Freethought Publishing Company issued it in London at twopence. Besant and Charles Bradlaugh printed it at their Stonecutter Street address. The enquiry grows out of the trial of the Queen against Bradlaugh and Besant.

The question is legal. A ruling by the Lord Chief Justice in that trial defined obscene literature without regard to the publisher's motive. Besant asks whether the Bible falls within that ruling. If motive counts for nothing, she argues, then passages of scripture could be treated as obscene by the same test. The pamphlet presses the ruling's logic against the book its defenders held sacred. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
38970-phil-bradley-s-snow-shoe-trail-or-:
Phil Bradley's Snow-Shoe Trail is a boys' outdoor novel by Silas Boone, printed at New York in 1915. It belongs to the Mountain Boys series. Its subtitle sets the scene: the mountain boys in Canada wilds. A front plate shows the boys reading sign in the snow.

The first chapter goes into the land of the moose and caribou. The boys fish through the ice with tip-ups and sit beside a fragrant camp fire. Lub gets a bear, and X-Ray straps on his snow-shoes and reads a trail. A quarrel over game, a waif of the snow forest, and the mystery of the pine woods build the plot. A dance given by James Bodman and Baylay's homecoming close it. The book is brisk winter adventure for its young audience.
40286-the-decoration-of-leather-from-the:
The Decoration of Leather is a craft manual translated from the French of Georges de Recy by Maude Nathan, published in London by Constable in 1905. Illustrations and examples of leather decoration from various sources fill the book. Its first plate shows a blind-stamped leather binding of the twelfth century, the Winchester Domesday Book.

The translator's note explains the author's claim. In a preface left out of the translation, de Recy claims a place for his work between two kinds of books. On one side stand the books on the history and development of leather working. On the other stand the practical manuals of the workshop. His book joins the two. It treats the art of tooled, stamped, and gilded leather, from medieval bindings to the bookbinding revival of his own day. It is told for craftsmen who wanted both the story and the method.
40403-girls-of-highland-hall-further-adv:
Girls of Highland Hall, further adventures of the Dandelion cottagers, is a school story by Carroll Watson Rankin, published by Henry Holt at New York in 1921. Rankin had already written Dandelion Cottage, the Girls of Gardenville, and the Cinder Pond.

The contents promise the journey and first impressions, then strange disappearances and many small mysteries, Mabel finding a family, unpopular Marjory, a surprising festival, and a string of blue beads. Later chapters bring a girl leaving school, a mystery cleared, a surprising question of pig or pork, and an exciting father. The story opens near noon on a warm September day on State Street, Chicago, with six persons walking two by two, four of them seeing the city for the first time.
40511-commander-lawless-v-c:
Commander Lawless is a naval adventure tale by Rolf Bennett, issued at London and New York in nineteen sixteen. Its subtitle promises the further adventures of Frank H Lawless, lately a lieutenant in the navy. Bennett also wrote Captain Calamity, his title page notes. Contents run to nine chapters, from The Night Attack to Abandon Ship.

Chapter one finds Flight Lieutenant Lawless in a large shed, watching his mechanic clean a monoplane's engines. He sucks at an empty pipe with a gloomy face. Misfortune has dogged him since his transfer to the flying wing, the tale says. He suffers violent air sickness that grows worse with time. Only his mechanic shares that shameful secret. He has also smashed up two monoplanes, the chapter adds.
41146-club-life-of-london-vol-1-of-2-wit:
John Timbs collects Club Life of London, volume 1 of 2, printed in London in 1866. Bentley made the book. Its full title promises anecdotes of the clubs, coffee houses, and taverns of the metropolis. The span is the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries.

His preface owns that pictures of London social life are by no means rare. Diaries, memoirs, and letters hold them in countless volumes, he says. They sparkle with humour and gaiety, and turn grave with politics as the age turns. A plate of Captain Charles Morris fronts the text. Club men and coffee house wits fill a fat, fond record of town nights.
41516-club-life-of-london-vol-2-of-2-wit:
John Timbs gathered this second volume on London club life, published by Bentley in 1866. The full work promises tales of the clubs, coffee-houses and taverns of the city in the seventeenth, eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Volume two opens with coffee-houses, starting with the early houses of the trade.

Garraway's, Jonathan's, the Rainbow, Nando's and Dick's each get a short section in turn. The famous Lloyd's coffee-house appears in the list as well. Timbs mixes names, dates and small stories to show how drink, news, trade and talk built a social world in old London rooms.
41800-the-treaty-of-waitangi-or-how-new-:
Lindsay Buick wrote The Treaty of Waitangi, or how New Zealand became a British colony, printed at Wellington in 1914. Buick had written Old Marlborough and An Old New Zealander. A front picture shows the commemorative monument, on which the articles of the treaty are engraved, so that eyes may look thereon from year to year. Buick gives the book to Robert McNab, to whose enterprise we owe the recovery of so much of our fast receding history.

A note of thanks names the author's helpers. Charles Wilson, librarian to the New Zealand Parliament, let him freely examine the rare official papers he wished to consult. Hamilton of the Dominion Museum opened the museum's New Zealand books to him. Others helped with the Hocken Collection at Dunedin. The text holds quotations from the instructions to Captain Hobson in 1839.
42037-notes-and-queries-number-135-may-2:
Notes and Queries, number 135 of volume 5, is the issue of Saturday, May 29, 1852, a medium of inter communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Captain Cuttle's saying stands as its motto: when found, make a note of. The price is fourpence.

The lead note prints a journal of the expenses of John, king of France, in England in 1359 and 1360, the captive taken by the Black Prince. Queries ask after the etymology of the word devil, a forged papal seal, a passage in All's Well That Ends Well, and surnames. Minor queries range from the bishop of Saint Asaph to will o' the wisps and market crosses. Replies treat Addison and his hymns, witchcraft, dodo queries, ground ice, and the character of Algernon Sydney. A miscellaneous tail of book notices, volumes wanted, and notices to correspondents closes the number.
42621-poems-containing-the-restropect-od:
Robert Lovell and Robert Southey, both young men of Balliol College, Oxford, joined their verse in this small book. Cruttwell printed it at Bath in 1795, and Dilly sold it in London for three shillings and sixpence. The Retrospect heads the title's list of forms.

Odes, elegies, and sonnets fill the book, with The Death of Mattathias among the named pieces. A Horace motto heads the title page: that black cares shrink under song. The preface borrows a quaint old hand of 1633 to plead the book's case. Two friends at the start of their paths share these pages; Southey would grow into a famed poet of his age.
42818-notes-and-queries-number-240-june-:
Notes and Queries, number 240, is the issue for Saturday, June 3, 1854. The weekly styled itself a medium of inter-communication. Literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists were its public. Captain Cuttle's saying serves as motto: when found, make a note of. The price was fourpence, or fivepence for the stamped edition. Four departments structure every number.

Notes open the issue, led by St Augustine on clairvoyance. J E B Mayor writes that note at page 511. Edward Gibbon, father and son, and Bohn's Ordericus Vitalis follow. Minor notes add inscriptions and register extracts. Queries ask about sepulchral monuments and South's sermons. Minor queries range from the spinning-machine of the ancients to Pope and Dennis. Replies answer earlier numbers: Julius III, Major André, and the terminations -by and -ness. Photographic correspondence reports collodion cautions and Fox Talbot's patents. Books wanted and notices to correspondents close the paper.
43559-fifth-report-of-the-vestry-of-the-:
The vestry of the parish of Chelsea in London made its fifth yearly report in 1861. The board sat under the Metropolis Local Management Act of 1855. Thirty seven appendices stand behind the report proper, and they hold the meat of the book.

Lists of vestrymen, auditors, and officers come first, with plans of the wards. Works and revenue follow. Chelsea Bridge Road takes pages of its own. Lighting, dust removal, and slaughter houses each have their returns. The vestry hall fills a long section, and the act itself is weighed for amendment. Charities, Cremorne Gardens, and the Thames embankment close the list, with a count of houses and people in 1851 and 1861.
44594-explanatory-notes-of-a-pack-of-cav:
Explanatory Notes of a Pack of Cavalier Playing Cards, by Edmund Goldsmid, was printed at Edinburgh in 1886. The pack dates from the time of Charles the Second. Goldsmid shows that the fifty two cards form a full political satire on the Commonwealth.

Lord Nelson let the rare pack be copied in facsimile for the Aungervyle Society of Edinburgh. Goldsmid tells how the cost of new copper plates was far past the means of a small society. Two societies joined funds to do the work right. His notes unpack each card, its figures, and its jabs at the men and events of the civil war age. Card fans and past buffs get a rare print toy read in full.
44615-siam-its-government-manners-custom:
Siam: Its Government, Manners, Customs, by McDonald, was published at Philadelphia in 1871. McDonald had been a missionary in Siam for ten years. He gives the little volume to the memory of the founder of Milnwood Academy, and to all who had been pupils there.

Chapters treat geography first, then government, religion, and education and literature. Manners and customs, courtship and marriage, and ceremonies for the dying and dead follow. Medicine in theory and practice, farming and products, and the mode of dividing time come next. Missionary operations close the book. In his preface McDonald says the pages began as lectures at Milnwood Academy, at Shade Gap. Friends asked that the talks be put to paper. Readers get a missionary plain account of Siam, from a decade of living there.
44989-the-complete-cynic-being-bunches-o:
The Complete Cynic, subtitled Bunches of Wisdom Culled from the Calendars, came from Oliver Herford, Ethel Watts Mumford, and Addison Mizner. It was published at San Francisco, with parts under copyright from 1902 onward. Three fond dedications open the book, one of them to the merry.

Herford rhyme for 1905 gives the book to the world at large, that rampageous reprobate. Pictures at the front show the first Monday, the first fashion plate, and the first lesson. Short, sharp sayings are the stock of the calendars from which the wisdom was culled. Readers get a small book of wit and mock wisdom, light in tone and meant to raise a smile rather than to teach a lesson.
4675-the-sea-witch-or-the-african-quadro:
Lieutenant Murray wrote The Sea-Witch, or The African Quadroon, as a story of the slave coast, published at New York with other short tales bound in. Its contents run from Outward Bound and Captain Will Ratlin, through the gale, Bramble Park, the naval officer, and the wreck, to the Sea Witch herself and the quadroon. An attack, a duel, hues of love, a conflict, and a trial follow.

Later chapters add brothers, an escape, cannibals, a poisoned barb, and a denouement. Murray's preface asks readers not to take the book as a pro-slavery or anti-slavery tale, since slavery enters only where plot and locality require it. Readers get a sea adventure of its day, with wreck, pursuit, and romance on the African coast, plus extra stories by other hands in the same volume.
4678-lives-of-the-english-poets-gay-thom:
Samuel Johnson's Lives of the English Poets appears here in a volume covering Gay, Thomson, Young, Gray, and others, transcribed from the 1889 Cassell edition. The introduction says this volume records twenty lives, of which only Edward Young's is treated at length. It completes the edition of Johnson's Lives, from which only a few of the briefest and least important lives have been omitted.

The eldest poets discussed are Samuel Garth, Charles Montague, Lord Halifax, and William King, born in 1660 to 1663. Next come Ambrose Philips, friend of Addison, and Nicholas Rowe, dramatist and first editor of Shakespeare after the four folios, born in 1671 and 1673. Isaac Watts follows, born in 1674, then Thomas Parnell, born in 1679, nearly of like age with Young, born in 1681. Readers get Johnson's sharp, compact biographies, rich in judgement.
47580-birds-and-all-nature-vol-4-no-2-au:
Birds and All Nature, volume four number two, is an illustrated nature magazine from August 1898. Its pages are illustrated by colour photography, the cover states. The contents open with an essay called Nature's Adjustments. Pieces on the reasoning powers of birds and a squirrel's road follow. The common tern, the prairie wolf, and the fox squirrel are treated. The loon, the mockingbird, and the bobolink also appear.

Other pieces ask how butterflies are protected in nature. The red fox, the least sandpiper, and the mountain sheep get articles. One piece describes a seminary for teaching birds how to sing. The first essay argues that nature's ways are held to be just right. It likens doubters to a farmer who refused a lightning rod. The issue mixes short animal studies with verse and notes. It shows how popular natural history was packaged for homes.
47884-birds-and-nature-vol-12-no-4-septe:
Birds and Nature issued a November 1902 number, volume twelve, number four, shown by color photography, despite the September date in its catalog title. A November poem opens the issue, full of frost, thistle down, and partridge drumming. The pileated woodpecker gets the first long article. The starling and the Arkansas goldfinch follow.

Short pieces cover building for bird tenants and tragedy in bird life. The black bellied plover, the diamond, and the horned toads appear. One writer describes a pet bat, and another treats the atlas moth. Vines of the wild woods and the egg plant close the number. Verse and prose mix throughout.
48523-birds-and-nature-vol-08-no-2-septe:
Birds and Nature for September 1900 is an issue of a magazine illustrated by colour photography. Mumford held its copyright. A poem by Helen Hunt Jackson opens the number, on goldenrod and turning corn. The mallows get the first article, treating the whole mallow family. Common mallow, velvet leaf, and marsh mallow are described in turn. Eagle lore and the snowdrop's philosophy follow.

Flowers and their invited guests treats how blooms draw insects. Asters, school gardens, and tiger lilies fill the middle pages. What Do We Owe the Birds asks its title question outright. The vesper sparrow and the Oregon junco get bird studies of their own. Fish close the issue: the calico bass, the growth of fish, and the origin of fish. Nature verse and plain science mix throughout.
49618-faith-and-duty-sermons-on-free-tex:
Louis Buchheimer, pastor of a Lutheran church in Saint Louis, gathers sermons in Faith and Duty. Concordia Publishing House of Saint Louis printed the book in 1913. The sub title calls them sermons on free texts, keyed to the church year.

The list runs with the church calendar. Advent Sundays open the year, each with a Bible text of its own. Christmas, New Year, and Epiphany follow in turn. Lent texts then lead the long march of Sundays. Each sermon takes one short text and works it for faith and duty. Church folk get a full year of plain, text based preaching.
51042-the-nakimu-caves-glacier-dominion-:
The Nakimu Caves is a pamphlet on a set of caves in Glacier Dominion Park, British Columbia. It was issued at Ottawa in 1914 by the Dominion Parks Branch of the Department of the Interior. A picture of the road to the caves, with Ross Peak in the centre, stands at the front.

The caves lie near the top of the Selkirk range, in the bed of Cougar Creek. They were new found when the pamphlet was made, and hard to reach. Fewer than a thousand visitors a year made the trip. The substance rests on two men. One is Wheeler, founder of the Canadian Alpine Club, who described the caves. The other is Ayres, a mining engineer sent to report on them. A road being built would open the caves to all, seven miles by pony from the railway hotel at Glacier.
51302-english-coins-and-tokens-with-a-ch:
English Coins and Tokens, by Llewellynn Jewitt, was published in London in 1886. Jewitt had also written The Ceramic Art of Great Britain and works on grave mounds and stately homes. A chapter on Greek and Roman coins is by Barclay Head, assistant keeper of coins at the British Museum.

The book opens with the coins of the ancient Britons. Jewitt says no one can say with certainty when the art of coining was first learned in Britain. He argues it most likely came from Gaul, and that Kent, nearest that land, knew money first. Kentish folk traded with Belgic tribes across the water. Readers get a Victorian guide to British money, from its first rude coins to tokens.
52347-the-cornplanter-memorial-an-histor:
James Snowden wrote this sketch of Cornplanter and the Six Nations of Indians. Pennsylvania ordered the book printed at Harrisburg in 1867. Samuel Johnson reports on a monument raised at Jennesadaga to Cornplanter. The state senate voted thanks to both men for the work.

One thousand copies of report and sketch were ordered printed then. Snowden gave his address in the House hall on March 14, 1867. Members of both houses and citizens filled the hall that day. The book honors a famed Seneca chief and his peoples long history. James Ross Snowden wrote the sketch of the chief.
5263-the-girl-scout-pioneers-or-winning-:
Lillian C. Garis's Girl Scout Pioneers follows a troop of Girl Scouts working to win their first badge, here called the first B. C. Chapters move from girls and girls and woodland thrills through a noble deed undone, paths dividing, a friendly enemy, a novel jail. Tenderfoot adventures follow, toward a clue to the missing and a tribute of roses.

Garis, author of several Girl Scout books, writes cheerful stories of camping, teamwork, and pluck. The book offers young readers an early portrait of the Girl Scouts in action, with mysteries, woodland magic. The flying squadron carries the troop toward its goal.
52973-geology-and-revelation-or-the-anci:
Geology and Revelation, by Gerald Molloy, was issued in New York in 1870. Molloy taught theology at St Patrick's College, Maynooth. A quote from Saint Thomas in Latin heads the book. In English it runs: hold fast to the truth of Scripture, yet cling to no one reading of it. If a reading proves false, do not insist, lest unbelievers mock. An added chapter on cosmogony comes from Professor Dana's manual of geology.

Molloy says new science raised sharp doubts against revealed truth. None took hold in England and Europe like the finds of geology, he argues. The book weighs the ancient history of the earth against geological facts. It seeks room for both the rocks and the Bible, in a careful Catholic frame.
53324-tales-of-the-r-i-c:
Tales of the RIC came out at Edinburgh in 1921, a set of twenty-one stories of the Irish police. Tall tales and grave ones stand side by side: The Informer, On the Run, The Landing of Arms, and A Brutal Murder.

The first tale follows Patsey Mulligan, one of ten children on a small mountain farm in the west of Ireland. Work drives him to a Yorkshire coal mine, and war sends him to the trenches at Ypres under another name. Later tales treat poteen, a bog cemetery, mountain warfare, and the truce. The voice is that of men who served through the troubles.
53954-william-morris-to-whistler-papers-:
William Morris to Whistler gathers papers and addresses on art and craft by Walter Crane, printed in London in 1911. Crane designed the title page, end papers, and cover. Plates show Morris designs for wall paper, hangings, and cotton prints. One sketch shows Morris speaking from a wagon in Hyde Park. The contents run from Morris and his work to art and the commonweal.

Essays treat the English revival in decorative art and the socialist ideal in art. Others cover the study of art, colour embroidery, and early Italian gesso work. Crane also writes on animals in art and on beauty in modern life. A survey of art in the nineteenth century closes the main text.
54276-physiology-and-histology-of-the-cu:
Physiology and Histology of the Cubomedusae is a thesis by E W Berger. It was shown to the board of Johns Hopkins University for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy and printed at Baltimore in 1900. It stands in the Memoirs from the Biological Laboratory, and it holds work of two men. Franklin Story Conant began the study of these box jellies and left notes of his tests. His kin paid to print the book as a mark of his worth.

Berger worked Conant's stock of beasts into fresh results. Tests treat how Charybdea meets light and dark, its sense clubs, stomach, and sting threads. Fine cuts of the beast's eye, with lens and retina, fill the back. Sea fans get a close, grave study of one of the sea's most strange and stinging kin.
54278-proclamation-of-the-twelve-apostle:
The Twelve Apostles of the Latter-Day Saints sent a loud call to all lands. It speaks to kings, to the chief of the United States, and to all folk. Know ye that the kingdom of God has come, it crows. Old seers told of that kingdom, and all ages prayed for it. It shall fill the whole earth and stand for ever, it holds.

God has spoke from the skies once more, the call claims. Sight and holy guests have borne His word to men anew. The high priesthood is back on earth by that gift. Its keys bind and loose on earth as in the skies. Saints hold this call as a key stone of faith.
54515-instructions-for-officers-and-non-:
Instructions for Officers and Non-Commissioned Officers of Cavalry on Outpost Duty was reprinted at Richmond, Virginia, in 1861 from the London edition. Von Arentschildt of the First Hussars, King's German Legion, wrote the manual, and Ponsonby of the Twelfth Light Dragoons shortened it.

Philip Cocke, commanding the Potomac Military Department of Virginia, ordered the reprint and dedicated it to Captain Lay and his Powhatan Troop. The lessons begin with parading the picquet: names written down, arms and ammunition inspected, men loaded, forage and provisions checked. Then come the march out, the choice of a stand behind a bridge, a ravine or between bogs, and the posting of videttes by day.
55558-the-boarding-school-lessons-of-a-p:
Hannah Foster, named only as a lady of Massachusetts and the author of The Coquette, sets out how young women should behave. J P Peaslee issued the book at Boston in 1829. Letters written by the pupils close the volume.

The frame story places a school on the banks of the Merrimac. Mrs Williams, a clergyman's widow, keeps it there. She has two lovely daughters of her own. Her means are easy, thanks to a small patrimony. She opens the school to guard that fund for her children. She also hopes to widen their society. The dedication speaks straight to the young ladies of America. It argues that a useful, happy life starts with principles learned young. Such preceptress books shaped early American girlhood.
55705-canoe-and-camp-cookery-a-practical:
Canoe and Camp Cookery is a practical cook book by a writer calling himself Seneca. The Forest and Stream Publishing Company issued it in New York in 1885. Its readers are named on the title page in the slang of the day. Canoeists, Corinthian sailors, and outers of every kind are addressed.

The first part treats cooking on a canoe cruise in detail. One receptacle, the grub box, should hold all that a meal requires. Soups, fish, meats, and game fill the teaching chapters in turn. Fish should be killed as soon as caught, the book directs. Pigeons, squirrels, ducks, and even frogs enter the game list. Coffee, johnnycake, slapjacks, and camp bread close the canoe section. The camp part adds ranges built outdoors, fuel, and the washing of dishes.
56167-the-viking-age-volume-1-of-2-the-e:
The Viking Age is a two volume work on the early Northmen by Paul Du Chaillu, published in eighteen eighty nine. Volume one carries more than thirteen hundred pictures and a map in all. Its front plate shows the Gokstad ship, used for burial in Norway. The subtitle calls the Norse the ancestors of the English speaking nations.

Du Chaillu draws his matter from finds in mounds, cairns, and bogs in the North. The sagas and eddas of the old North give him the rest of his proof. In the preface he asks why English speakers spread so far across the globe. He asks whence their energy, daring, and gift for self rule came down. The Romans, he notes, found no such traits in the Britons they invaded. His answer traces those traits to the Viking forebears of the English.
56168-the-viking-age-volume-2-of-2-the-e:
Paul du Chaillu wrote a two-volume history of the Viking Age, drawn from finds in mounds, cairns, and bogs and from the ancient sagas and Eddas. This second volume, issued at New York in 1889, carries 1366 illustrations and a map. Its frontispiece shows a bronze-covered waggon found in a Jutland bog.

The contents open with marriage, divorce, and the bringing-up of children, then pass to weapons and war customs. War-ships, fleets, and sea battles give way to halls, feasts, and the dress of men and women. Poetry and scalds, the conduct of life in the Hávamál, and the deeds of great Vikings close the volume. English-speaking readers tracing their ancestors were the audience.
56229-the-young-wireless-operator-with-t:
The Young Wireless Operator with the Oyster Fleet, by Lewis E Theiss, was printed by W A Wilde with a copyright of 1922 and art by Frank T Merrill. Its sub claim names the arc: how Alec Cunningham won his way to the top in the oyster trade. The tale opens at Bivalve, the great New Jersey oyster port, on a black November dawn. The boat Bertha B lies packed with the fleet in the Maurice River while the tide runs out hard.

Heads ahead name the fleet's sail, the run over the bar, and the dredge work. A man goes over in the dark, a cloud falls on Alec, and a wireless phone set joins the gear. Storms strand the crew before the close. Boys of the age got salt work, sparks, and grit in one hull.
56471-corporal-tikitanu-v-c:
J C Fussell tells the story of Henare Tikitanu in Corporal Tikitanu, V C, printed at Auckland in 1918 as a sequel to his Letters from Private Henare Tikitanu. The eight chapters run from elopement to enlistment, through a little French nurse and a letter to the Kaiser. A later chapter shows the corporal earning the Victoria Cross, and the last brings the homecoming.

The narrator first saw Henare refereeing a dog-fight in a Maori village in the Waikato district, about two years before the Great War. Henare, then eighteen, is now torn between enlisting among the first volunteers and secretly marrying his sweetheart Kiri, whom the rival Wiremu also courts.
56674-a-catalogue-of-technical-and-scien:
Constable of London issued a catalogue of its technical and scientific books in 1921, from its house in Orange Street by Leicester Square. The list is sorted by subject, and each trade has its own page. A note at the front fixes the cost of posting books inland. Prices, it warns, may change without notice as costs rise and fall.

The heads of the list map the whole of applied science in that age. They run from flying and farming to civil works, electric power, and fuel. Iron and steel, engines, pumps, mines, and railways each have their place. Later heads treat town works, mathematics, natural history, physics, and chemistry. Series of books are listed apart, among them works on the trades, on health in camp, and on industrial chemistry. The catalogue is a shop window for the engineer, the builder, and the student of 1921.
56830-the-flags-of-our-fighting-army-inc:
Stanley Johnson wrote this guide to flags of the British fighting army. Black printed it in London in 1918 with eight color plates. Johnson gives the book to his brother in the Royal Garrison Artillery. Early plates show regimental colors and old standards from 1687 onward.

Contents start with an introduction and a history of military colors. Standards and guidons of horse troops take the next chapter. Foot Guards and infantry colors fill the long core of the book. Colors of overseas dominions, odd colors, and battle honours close the book for reference use.
57541-index-for-works-of-willis-george-e:
David Widger compiled this index for the works of Willis George Emerson, with links to all the contents. Five books stand in the main list, plus a piece called On Sound Money. The books are The Smoky God, A Vendetta of the Hills, Buell Hampton, My Pardner and I, and The Treasure of Hidden Valley. Full contents follow for each book in turn.

For The Smoky God, the parts trace Olaf Jansen's story beyond the north wind, in the under world, and among the ice packs. A Vendetta of the Hills runs to wedding bells through quarrels, jail, and a fight on a cliff. Buell Hampton opens at Lake Geneva and moves to a frontier banker and a cattle king. The index lets readers scan each plot at a glance.
58823-the-scottish-journal-of-topography:
The Scottish Journal, number 22, is dated at Edinburgh, January 29, 1848. Its full title adds topography, antiquities, and traditions. The price was one penny halfpenny. A family history leads the number. Joseph Train copied the account from a manuscript held by Dr Thomson, late of Appin. It treats the family of Invernahyle. Alexander, the first of the line, was son to Allan Stewart, third laird of Appin. One summer morning he crossed to a small isle, his Lochaber axe by him. A deadly feud stood between his house and Dunstaffnage.

Colin of Dunstaffnage landed unseen and masked his purpose in friendship. Seeing Alexander defenceless, he grasped at the axe. Both men seized it, and Colin's men closed in and murdered him. His infant son Donald was suckled by Morag, a Moidart woman, who fled with the child.
59133-a-body-of-divinity-vol-1-of-4-wher:
Thomas Ridgley's lectures on the Larger Catechism fill four volumes, and volume one is the first American printing, from the third European edition, issued at Philadelphia in 1814. James P Wilson added notes, his own and chosen from others.

Ridgley works through the doctrines of the Christian religion point by point, explaining and defending each as the Assembly's catechism states it. The opening pages carry the 1813 copyright entry made by the publisher William W Woodward, a mark of how such books were guarded at the time. Dissenting churches on both sides of the Atlantic used Ridgley as a standard guide. This edition put the whole course of lectures within reach of American readers, in their own print.
59532-the-glory-that-was-greece-a-survey:
J C Stobart, late lecturer in history at Trinity College, Cambridge, wrote this survey of Hellenic culture and civilization, published in London in 1911 with hundreds of illustrations. A companion volume, The Grandeur That Was Rome, was announced alongside.

The contents open with Hellenism, the land and its people, then pass to Aegean civilization: Crete, Mycenae, and Tiryns. The heroic age follows, then ages of transition with Sparta and Ionia. The grand century chapter takes in Pheidias, the temple-builders, tragedy, and comedy. Later come the fourth century, Alexander, and Alexandria, with a glossary and bibliography. The frontispiece is the Aphrodite of Melos. General readers get Greece whole, in one richly pictured volume.
59652-cronus-of-the-d-f-c:
Lloyd Biggle wrote a tale of crime and time called Cronus of the D F C, first run in Worlds of If in February 1957. A new hand named Forsdon joins a strange police unit housed in a basement room full of tubes, wires, and dials. Its chief, Captain Marks, is a hard eyed old detective who held on past the age to retire.

The unit is the Department of Future Crime, a costly trial tool that the brass may yet scrap. Its gear can show crimes still days away. The head note tells the twist: Forsdon falls in love with a woman he has seen marked for murder in five days. The tale mixes police work with a race against a fixed fate.
60277-ae-rial-navigation-a-popular-treat:
Aerial Navigation, by Albert Francis Zahm, is a popular treatise on air craft. Appleton of New York and London issued the book in nineteen eleven. Zahm served the Aero Club of Washington and the Aero Club of America. He had taught mechanics at the Bureau of Standards and at Catholic University.

Part one traces the growth of balloons, free and powered, in detail. Gasoline driven dirigibles and stiff and soft airships earn their own chapters. Part two turns to aviation, from model flyers to man carrying planes. Public flying and contest flying close that growth survey in the book. Part three treats the weather of the free air for airmen.
61071-the-constitutional-amendment-or-th:
Littlejohn, a Seventh-day Adventist, debates the editor of the Christian Statesman in this volume of 1873. Its full title names a proposed amendment, the Sunday, the Sabbath, the change, and restitution. The Steam Press of the Adventist firm at Battle Creek, Michigan, made the book. Most parts had run in the Christian Statesman, the Sabbath Recorder, and the Advent Review. Wider circulation is the aim of this bound form.

A party had formed to amend the Constitution of the United States, the preface says. Its aims were to put the names of God and Christ in that charter. It sought the Bible named as the fountain of national law as well. Bible reading in the common schools and Sunday laws stand in the same program. Littlejohn argues the Sabbath side against that push, point by point.
62149-a-body-of-divinity-vol-2-of-4-wher:
A Body of Divinity, volume two, is a theological work by Thomas Ridgley. James Wilson added notes, original and selected, to this edition. Woodward printed it at Philadelphia in 1815. It is the first American issue from the third European edition. The whole work fills four volumes in all. Its subtitle says the doctrines of the Christian religion are explained and defended. The lectures rest on the Assembly's Larger Catechism. The contents of this volume begin with creation.

Questions fourteen and fifteen treat the work of creation. Creation was not from eternity, the heads argue. It was performed in six days by God's power and for his glory. Questions on angels follow, covering their nature and employment. The creation of man comes next in the contents. Man was created male and female in God's image. The volume is a catechism commentary in systematic form.
62188-betty-crocker-s-frosting-secrets-f:
Betty Crocker's Frosting Secrets is a General Mills booklet of 1958. Its cover lines promise fancy cake decorating and new trimming short cuts. Contents list the lessons by page. Quick frosting tricks come first: teaspoon scallops, spatula spirals, and crisscross. A cherry blossom cake and easy flowers follow. Party cakes fill the middle: forget-me-not, trellis, daisy, and gift wrapped cakes. Birthday cakes, a doll cake, and petit fours come next. Holiday cakes include a sugarplum tree, an Easter bonnet, and a valentine. A wedding cake stands at page twenty.

A welcome letter signed Betty Crocker opens the teaching. Frosting mix, she says, makes decorator icing smooth and easy-flowing. First cakes need no special tools: fork, spoon, spatula, or string can make frosting fancy. Plain tips come first: cool the cake, brush crumbs away, frost the sides before the top.
62557-the-dominion-astrophysical-observa:
The Dominion Astrophysical Observatory, Victoria, is an official account by Plaskett, the observatory's director. The Department of the Interior issued it at Ottawa in 1923. Its title page promises three things in one sketch. It gives the development of astronomy in Canada first. It describes the building and the telescope's workings next. It ends with an account of the institution's principal work. A frontispiece shows the building and dome from the south. The staff list names research and assistant astronomers under Plaskett.

Section one treats the history and construction of the place. Astronomy in Canada grew from the needs of land survey, it explains. Boundary and township surveys demanded precise positions early on. The observatory is a branch of the department in charge of western lands. Plaskett writes as founder director reporting his institution.
6267-the-weavers-a-tale-of-england-and-e:
A quiet valley village, once a river bed in an age when the Thames flowed into the Seine, opens a novel that will travel to Cairo and back across fifty years. David Claridge leaves Hamley under a call, Faith waits and writes, Nahoum schemes in palaces, and Hylda seeks answers in bazaars. Six books carry the tale from a spirit moved and gates of the world through jehads, debts, desert struggles, and a loom of destiny.

Read whole, the novel joins an English Quaker household to Egyptian power, as David faces Kaid and Nahoum in palace rooms and Faith holds Hamley steady. Letters, compacts, and secrets bind the two worlds, and old wrongs return in desert and court alike. Parker writes a long romance of conscience and empire, where a village boy's calling reshapes a kingdom and costs him nearly everything he loves.
63641-the-new-york-tombs-inside-and-out-:
The New York Tombs Inside and Out is an exposé by John Josiah Munro, the prison's former chaplain. The subtitle promises scenes and reminiscences coming down to the present, a story stranger than fiction, with a history of the prison.

An introduction by a fellow minister vouches for Munro and urges that every citizen of Greater New York read him. The book, he says, will furnish material for sermons and give impetus to all workers for social betterment. Munro thanks the Christian Herald's editors and the New York papers that had printed his prison articles. The Tombs, the city prison in the old Halls of Justice, was a byword for damp cells and corruption, and its chaplain writes as a reformer with a ringside seat.
64396-the-private-life-the-wheel-of-time:
Henry James published a volume of six tales at London in 1893, containing The Private Life, The Wheel of Time, Lord Beaupré, The Visits, Collaboration, and Owen Wingrave. The Private Life opens in Switzerland, face to face with a great bristling, primeval glacier. The hour and scene, the narrator says, make up for the modern indignity of travel. The high valley is pink with the mountain rose.

The cool air is as fresh as if the world were young, James writes. The tales treat artists, ghosts, and social performance. Owen Wingrave, the last, is his famous ghost story of a soldier's son. Osgood, McIlvaine published the volume at Albemarle Street.
64653-biographical-catalogue-of-the-port:
Mary Louisa Boyle's Biographical Catalogue of the Portraits at Longleat, published by Elliot Stock in London in 1881, describes the portraits in the Wiltshire seat of the Marquis of Bath. Boyle, a kinswoman of the family, inscribes the book to the owners of that beautiful home, endeared to her by the friendship of three generations. She apologizes for uneven notices: she worked while traveling, short of reference books, and with failing sight.

The catalogue is a family record first. Notices of persons tied, even remotely, to the owners of Longleat get the fullest treatment, while kings and queens are usually given a few lines. She breaks that rule for the King and Queen of Bohemia, whose lives, she says, read as a romance. Her authorities are the great memoir writers, Clarendon, Burnet, Strype, and Aubrey among them, and Canon Jackson's local knowledge helped throughout.
65009-u-s-marine-operations-in-korea-195:
Lynn Montross and Captain Canzona wrote the third volume of Marine Operations in Korea. Its subject is the Chosin Reservoir campaign of 1950 to 1953. The Historical Branch at Marine Corps headquarters in Washington made the book in 1957. It sold for two dollars and seventy-five cents through the government printer. Two volumes came before it: the Pusan Perimeter and the Inchon-Seoul operation.

Contents open with problems of victory after the drive north. The decision to cross the thirty-eighth parallel and the Wonsan landing follow. Two weeks of mine sweeping earned the landing its yo-yo nickname. The first Marine division came ashore there under orders to advance to the border.
